analysis.one_liner: Requires large websites and apps to get users' express consent before collecting or selling their personal data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a single committee or floor action beyond referral, drew zero cosponsors, and died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The DATA Act would have required large websites, apps, and social networks — those with 30 million or more U.S. monthly users that use algorithms to rank or filter content — to get a user's express consent before collecting data about their habits, traits, preferences, beliefs, or location, or before selling or sharing that data with anyone else. Users could have withdrawn consent and demanded deletion of their data, and platforms would have had to say, in plain language, what data they take and exactly which third parties they sell or share it with. The Federal Trade Commission could have enforced the rules, and individual users could have sued violators for at least $5,000 plus attorney's fees.
analysis.who_benefits: The hundreds of millions of Americans who use large websites, social networks, video platforms, and search engines would gain control over what data about them gets collected and who it is sold to. The bill's notice rules would have forced platforms to disclose, by name and country, every third party receiving a user's data, and users could have revoked consent and had their data deleted. People harmed by violations could have sued for a minimum of $5,000 in damages plus attorney's fees, and the FTC could have treated violations as unfair or deceptive practices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Users of large websites and apps

how_it_helps.text: Platforms with 30 million or more U.S. monthly users that use ranking or filtering algorithms would have been barred from collecting data about a person's habits, traits, preferences, beliefs, or location without that person's express consent, and users could have revoked consent and demanded deletion.

Platforms would have been barred from selling, sharing, or conveying a user's covered data to third parties without express consent, and their notices would have had to name the specific data, the third parties receiving it, and those third parties' countries of origin.
The notice had to be in plain language, in a conspicuous manner, and repeated at each login unless the user waived it — not buried in a terms-of-service update.

Enforcement would have come from two directions: the FTC treating violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and a private right of action letting any individual sue in state or federal court, with a statutory minimum award of $5,000, actual damages if greater, and attorney's fees and costs for prevailing plaintiffs.

analysis.who_pays: Large internet platforms — social networks, video services, ad networks, search engines, mobile operating systems, email services, and internet providers with 30 million or more U.S. users — would have borne the cost of rewriting data practices around consent, processing deletion and revocation requests, and displaying recurring plain-language notices. The ad-tech and data-broker ecosystem that buys and sells user data would have lost access to data that users declined to share, and platforms would have faced FTC penalties and private lawsuits carrying a $5,000 minimum per violation.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action with a $5,000 statutory minimum award per violation and guaranteed attorney's fees could have generated a wave of lawsuits over notice or consent paperwork errors, even where no user was concretely harmed beyond the formality of a missed disclosure.

The bill defines a covered platform as any site with 30 million U.S. users that uses an algorithm to increase or decrease the availability of content — a definition broad enough to cover nearly every major website and app, since virtually all of them rank or filter content — so compliance costs and repeated login notices would have fallen on the whole large-platform sector at once.

The term 'covered data' (habits, traits, preferences, beliefs, or location) and 'express consent' are not further defined in the bill, leaving the FTC to fill in the details by rule and creating uncertainty for platforms and courts alike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — giving users a genuine say over whether their behavioral data is collected and sold, with named third-party disclosures — addresses one of the most common complaints about the internet economy and mirrors consent regimes already in force in states like California and in Europe. The costs are real: near-universal compliance burdens on large platforms, recurring consent friction, and a lawsuit-friendly enforcement design whose $5,000-per-violation floor invites litigation over paperwork rather than harm. A better-drafted bill could have achieved the consent and disclosure goals with clearer definitions and a more carefully scoped private right of action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never held it over for a vote or sent it to the floor, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Rick Scott introduced the bill on April 29, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation.
That was the last action ever taken: the bill drew no cosponsors and the committee never reported it out or scheduled any hearing or vote on it during the two-year Congress.
The bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large internet platforms and the ad-tech and data-broker ecosystem that buys and sells user behavioral data are better off, because no consent, deletion, or third-party disclosure requirements were ever imposed on them.

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its sole sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 29, 2021 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: All other 99 senators
against.what_they_did: No senator from either party cosponsored the bill, and none acted to bring it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split on the bill itself can be measured; its single sponsor was a Republican.

industries.industry: Large social media and internet platforms
industries.note: The bill would have required any platform with 30 million or more U.S. users to get express consent before collecting or sharing behavioral data, honor deletion requests, and disclose third-party recipients by name and country — a direct cost to the advertising-driven business model. Because the bill died in committee, these platforms kept collecting and monetizing user data with no new federal consent requirement.

Companies that buy and sell user data would have lost access to any data whose owner withheld consent, and their receipt of data would have had to be disclosed to users by name and country of origin. The bill's death left their supply of behavioral data untouched.

The bill's private right of action with a $5,000 minimum award, attorney's fees, and a statutory declaration that any violation is a concrete injury would have created a new stream of privacy litigation. Whether that serves users depends on whether suits target real violations or paperwork technicalities.
